The glycidylic esters of alkylo- and methylphosphorus acids have been found to be anticholinesterases, narcotizing agents, and antineoplastics.
the toxicity and biological effects (anticholinesterase activity and antitumor activity) of organophosphororganic epoxids depends on the structure of the organic part of the molecule.

the biological effects of the organophosphorus compounds possessing the epoxy group, which are the products of the interaction of phosphoric and phosphonic acids with ethylene oxide, and which have not been studied earlier.
the biological activity and toxicity of the compounds studied, the mechanism of their action, and the possibility of their application in oncology.
the study of the biological properties of the compounds of a new class, the glycidylic phosphoric and methylphosporic acid esters.

the glycidylic phosphates studied are not of value as therapeutic agents.

the biological activity of organophosphororganic epoxdes is not only determined by the nature of the substituent in the phosphorus atom, but is also influenced by the nature of a second substituent in the carbon atom of the epoxy ring.

the toxicity and biological effects in relation to tumor cells of glycidylocylic ethers of phosphoric acid derivatives is dependent on the nature of the organic radical and the number of glycidyl groups in the molecule.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
monoglycidylyl ethers of diethylphosphoric acid and diglycidyl ethers of ethylphosphate are promising anticholinesterases.

the toxicity of the glycidylic esters of alkylphosphoric and alkylphosphonic acids is connected with the presence of an epoxide group, which is capable of forming a covalent bond with the cell components, and that the biological activity of the compounds depends upon the nature and the number of alkyl groups in the molecule.

the glycidylic phosphororganic compounds under study have the following biological activity: (1) anticholinesterases; (2) narcotics; (3) antineoplastic agents; (4) alkylating agents; and (5) agents causing the "hypnotic" syndrome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
organophosphorus compounds with the epoxide group in their structure can be used in chemotherapy of tumors.
organophosphorus compounds are capable of causing both cholinesterase and non-cholinesterase effects, and that these effects may be manifested in different ways.
glycidyl phosphates are highly toxic and have anticholinesterasic, narcotic, antineoplastic activities.
